Exercise 10 · Example. Do we need vowels? The Arabic child learns to read on vocalized texts; then the vowels disappear little by little, until there is very little left in the newspapers and books. Many people consider it normal: the experienced reader understands the word from context and does not need someone to vocalize it. Reality, however, is more complex. How many times has an experienced reader stopped in front of a word that can be read in two ways? How many times have we heard a conductor misread a news story, why did he only understand the sentence after it was over? I do not ask for everything to be vocalized: it would weigh down the text and slow down reading. However, I propose a solution in the middle: to vocalize the words that can confuse the reader, such as verbs to the passive and their rare names. Technology can help us: there are now automatic vocalization programs that give good results on simple texts. But they are still wrong when a knowledge of the world that the machine does not have is needed to understand: the program does not know that a book cannot chair a Union, nor that the referee who apologized to the public is a man and not a sentence. [N.d.T.: in Arabic, without vowels, ⁧الكتاب⁩ ), as an arbitrator and a judgment of the Court ( ⁧الحكم⁩ ]]" A creative solution without note is only possible if it retains the meaning (the problem of words with the same spelling).
